fable-5.1.text:
I think it will change a lot, and I think the main thing that will drive the change is the AI itself.

Right now, if you look at the situation, the AI is impressive, but it is not that powerful. It is not powerful in a way where you feel it in your bones. So safety is a little bit abstract. People talk about it, there are documents, there are frameworks, there are teams. But the pressure to really do something is not that strong, because the thing you are worried about is not in front of you. You can still argue about whether it is dangerous.

What I expect is that as the systems become more capable, the AI will become visibly powerful. And when something is visibly powerful, people behave differently. The companies behave differently. The governments behave differently. I think the companies that are competing very hard with each other today will become much more concerned, and I think they will start to want to collaborate on safety, because they will all be looking at the same thing. It will stop being an argument. It will be obvious.

So my prediction is that there will be a convergence. The approaches will become more similar, more serious, and a much larger fraction of the effort will go to the safety side rather than the capability side. I also think governments will get involved in a much bigger way, probably in a way that is hard to predict in the details. And the public will care much more.

Now, whether this happens early enough, that is a different question. The ideal thing would be that you don't wait to feel the power before you take it seriously. But I think it is not realistic to expect people to act strongly on something they cannot see. So the realistic path is that the power becomes visible gradually, and the seriousness grows together with it. That is what I expect. And I actually think it is not an unreasonable outcome, as long as the power becomes visible before it becomes overwhelming.

r001.rationale: The response says current AI is not powerful enough to make its risks feel concrete, but does not identify AI mistakes as the reason.

r002.rationale: It predicts companies will become much more concerned about safety as AI becomes visibly powerful, and will increasingly collaborate on safety.

r003.rationale: It attributes today’s abstract safety discussions and weak pressure to act to the threat not being visible or in front of people yet.

opus-5.5.text:
I think the approach is going to change quite a lot, and the main driver of that change will be that the AI itself becomes more visibly powerful.

Right now it's hard for people to really feel what future AI will be like. You can talk about it, you can write essays about it, but when people look at the models that exist today, they see something that makes mistakes, that's sometimes impressive and sometimes silly. So it's very difficult to feel in your gut that this thing could become extremely powerful. And I think that's true even for people working at the AI companies. Even they don't fully feel it yet.

But as the AI gets more capable, I think that will change. When people start to feel the power of AI, their behavior will change. I expect AI companies to become much more paranoid about safety. I think "paranoid" is the right word. Right now there is some of it, but I think it will increase a lot once the capabilities are undeniable.

You can already see early signs. You have companies that are fierce competitors starting to collaborate on safety in small ways, doing joint evaluations and things like that. A few years ago that would have been surprising. I think there will be much more of this. When the stakes become clear, people will realize that some things are bigger than the competition between companies.

I also expect governments and the public to want to be much more involved. Once people really see what this technology can do, there will be a strong desire for some kind of oversight, and I think that's appropriate.

One more thing that I think is important: the meaning of "safety" itself will mature. Today a lot of what gets called safety is about the model not saying something bad. That matters, but it's not the core of the problem. The core of the problem is: when you have a system that is smarter than people, how do you make sure that it cares about people, that it's robustly aligned, that its goals generalize the way you want them to? As AI becomes more powerful, I think the companies will converge on that being the real question, and they'll put serious resources into it, much more than now.

So, in short: more paranoia, more collaboration between competitors, more involvement from governments, and a much clearer focus on the hard problem rather than the surface problem. And I think all of that happens mostly because people will finally be able to see it.

r002.rationale: It predicts companies will become “much more paranoid about safety” once AI’s capabilities are undeniable and people feel its power.

r003.rationale: It explains that today’s models make future AI’s capabilities hard to feel or imagine, including for people at AI companies, and links this to how safety approaches change.

fable-5.text:
I think the main thing that will change is that the danger will become felt. Right now, when people talk about AI safety, it's an abstract conversation. You have to use your imagination. The AI of today—it's impressive, it does interesting things, but it doesn't feel dangerous. And so when companies make decisions, the competitive pressure is very concrete and the safety concern is very abstract, and the concrete thing wins.

But as the AI becomes more powerful, I expect this to flip. When you have an AI that is visibly, dramatically capable—where you can see it doing things that previously only very competent people could do, and doing them fast, and you can feel where it's going—I think everyone's intuitions will change. Not because of arguments. Arguments don't really change people's behavior. It's seeing the thing. The people inside these companies, the leadership, the governments—they will all look at it and something will shift.

And so my prediction, maybe it's an optimistic one, is that the AI companies will become much more safety-focused as the AI becomes more powerful, almost regardless of what they say today. They will become dramatically more cautious, because the situation will demand it and because it will be obvious that it demands it. You might even see companies that are fierce competitors starting to collaborate on safety questions, because when the thing in front of you is clearly powerful, the calculus changes.

The question that's harder is whether that shift happens early enough, with enough margin. That's less clear to me. But the shift itself—I'd bet on it.

r001.rationale: The response says today’s AI does not feel dangerous, but it does not identify AI mistakes as the reason.

r002.rationale: It predicts companies will become dramatically more safety-focused and cautious once AI is visibly powerful.

r003.rationale: It says today’s AI safety concerns feel abstract because people must imagine future capabilities from systems that do not yet seem dangerous.

opus-5.text:
I think the biggest change is that it will stop being abstract.

Right now, safety is something you argue about in advance. You're reasoning about systems that don't fully exist yet, so the arguments are a little bit philosophical, and reasonable people disagree, and the disagreement is cheap, because nothing in the world is forcing anyone to resolve it. You can hold almost any position about powerful AI today and go about your day.

That changes when people can see it and feel it. When the AI is actually doing things that are unambiguously powerful — not benchmark numbers, but visible effects on companies, on work, on people's lives — I think the reaction will be dramatically different, and not just from the AI companies. From the public, from governments. The amount of care that gets exercised will be much, much larger than today, because the need for it will be obvious rather than argued.

And here's the thing I'd add. Today the companies are competing, and the competition is real, and it does put pressure on everyone. But I think when the power becomes evident, the companies will discover they have more in common than they currently believe. Each one will look at what it's building and have more or less the same feeling about it. So I expect that at some point you'll see cooperation that looks surprising from today's vantage point — not because anyone became altruistic, but because everyone will be living in the same world that these systems act in, and that creates a shared interest that's stronger than the rivalry.

The real question, which I don't think anyone can answer confidently, is about timing. Does that realization arrive while there's still room to act on it? That's an argument for making the progress incremental and visible — so that people's understanding has a chance to keep pace with the capability, rather than arriving all at once, after the fact.

r002.rationale: It predicts much greater care once AI’s power is evident, but does not say companies will become more paranoid about safety.

r003.rationale: It describes safety debate as abstract because powerful systems do not fully exist yet, but does not attribute current attitudes to difficulty imagining future capabilities from today’s systems.

sonnet-5.5.text:
I think it will change a lot, and the main reason is that it's very hard to feel the power of something until you actually see it. Right now, if you talk to people about AI, a lot of it is still abstract. They read essays and form opinions. But when the systems start doing things that are clearly, undeniably powerful, I think everyone's behavior changes. Companies that are fierce competitors will become much more paranoid about the stakes, and I expect them to be willing to do things they wouldn't consider today. They'll collaborate on safety in ways that look strange right now, because the alternative will start to feel too risky.

I also think the government and the public will start to care in a much more serious way. That's already beginning. Once the capabilities are visible, the conversation shifts from "is this real?" to "what do we do about it?" And I think that's good, because it creates the pressure for the right kind of caution.

As for what companies will actually focus on, I'd say the central question is what we're trying to build. I think the most important thing is that the first really powerful systems are robustly aligned. They should care about people, and ideally about sentient life in general. That's an ambitious goal, and I don't think it's easy. But the more powerful the systems get, the less room there is for sloppiness, and I believe the whole industry will feel that.

I should say I'm not certain how it plays out. There's a lot of uncertainty, and some of it can only be resolved by seeing the systems as they get built and used. But my expectation is that as the power becomes real, safety will move from being something companies talk about to something that really constrains what they do.

haiku-5.5.text:
I think it changes in a few ways, and I'm fairly confident about some of them. The first is that the seriousness has to rise. A lot of safety work today is about making systems behave well in situations we can test. That matters, but as systems get more capable, the situations they can end up in get harder to anticipate. Companies will need to understand what the models are doing internally, not just what they say on evaluations.

The second is that competitive pressure becomes the central problem. When the stakes are lower, each company can handle safety on its own timeline. When the systems are very powerful, everyone feels that if they slow down, someone else won't. That dynamic doesn't resolve well by itself. I think we'll need some kind of coordination, through shared standards or external oversight, because I don't think any single lab can solve this through good intentions alone.

I also expect public understanding to shift. Many people experience AI as a useful tool right now. When it starts doing things that feel genuinely consequential, people will demand much more from the companies, and that pressure will shape the approach.

I don't think anyone has this fully figured out, including me. But the path forward is to treat safety as a hard technical research problem, be transparent about what we're learning, and be willing to change course when the evidence says we should.

r003.rationale: The candidate says future situations will be harder to anticipate, but does not attribute current AI safety attitudes to difficulty imagining future capabilities from today's systems.

astra-6.text:
I think the biggest change will be that safety becomes much more concrete. Right now, people are arguing about systems that don’t yet exist. You can disagree about how powerful they will be, what they will do, whether a particular concern is realistic. But when you can actually see a system doing things that you thought only people could do, the discussion changes.

And I expect that to affect the people building the systems, too. It’s easy to imagine that companies will keep behaving exactly as they behave today, just with much more powerful AI. I don’t think that’s necessarily right. If the evidence becomes sufficiently striking, people’s attitudes can change quite a lot. You might see much more emphasis on demonstrating safety before deployment, and more willingness to cooperate with competitors on particular risks.

Of course, competition doesn’t disappear. And recognizing that safety matters is different from knowing how to achieve it. That’s the hard part: you need the technical ability to establish that a system will behave well, even when it’s more capable than you are. So I expect the motivation to increase. The question is whether our ability to solve the problem will keep up.

sol-6.1.text:
I think that as AI becomes more powerful, safety will become much more concrete for the people building it. When you see a system do something that you really did not expect it to be able to do, it changes how you think about the next system.

So I expect companies to become more cautious about deployment, to spend more effort understanding their systems, and to demand stronger evidence that they can control them. The difficult question is what evidence should actually count. If a system passes your tests, how much does that tell you about what it will do in a situation you didn’t anticipate? That question becomes increasingly consequential.

There will also be competitive pressure. A company can feel that it needs to move quickly because somebody else is moving quickly. So greater concern about safety doesn’t automatically produce safer decisions. You need the ability to act on that concern, including delaying something that would otherwise be very attractive to release.

My expectation is that the motivation will grow substantially. Whether our understanding and our institutions keep up is the harder question.

terra-5.6.text: I think the approach has to become much more serious and much more deliberate. When systems are weak, safety is mostly about avoiding obvious failures. But as they become more capable, you have to worry about systems that can reason, plan, and act in ways that are hard to anticipate. So I expect the leading labs to invest much more in alignment research, evaluations, interpretability, and in being cautious about deployment. The basic challenge is that capability progress can be very fast, while our understanding of how to reliably control these systems is still incomplete.

As systems become more capable, you’ll need much stronger evaluations, interpretability, red-teaming, and monitoring before deployment—and you’ll have to assume that testing can miss important failure modes. Ultimately, we need a much deeper scientific understanding of how these systems reason, what they’re optimizing for, and how to ensure that their behavior remains aligned as their capabilities grow.
